roadmap.lecture_goal: design and implement an efficient algorithm for minimizing travel time in semi-interactive VR tours using graph theory and the Traveling Salesman Problem.

objectives.text: You'll be able to explain the principles of optimizing VR experience by controlling exposure duration and analyze the methods and trade-offs involved in managing VR exposure.
You'll be able to define the characteristics of semi-interactive VR tours and compare different optimization approaches for designing efficient VR tours.

You'll be able to model the optimal travel path problem by defining the graph structure and objective, deriving the travel time formula, and adapting the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for non-complete graphs.
You'll be able to describe and summarize the two-stage algorithm used to solve the TSP on a non-complete graph to minimize travel time.

segments.subgoal: Explain the approach of optimizing VR experience by controlling exposure duration

key_points.text: The lecture focuses on optimizing VR navigation experience, specifically by addressing cyber sickness concerns.
One optimization approach involves controlling the exposure duration to mitigate cyber sickness.
Cyber sickness symptoms are correlated to and rise proportionally with the duration of the VR session.
Shorter exposure duration is assumed to help minimize or eliminate the cyber sickness problem.

key_terms.definition: Optic flow is the rate at which the scenes change in the virtual world, which allows the user to perceive movement.
A system-controlled VR tour is a scenario where user movements and navigation are controlled by the system.
This approach involves optimizing cyber sickness by controlling the exposure duration.
Cyber sickness is correlated to the exposure duration in a VR environment, with symptoms rising proportionally to the session duration.

segments.subgoal: Analyze methods and trade-offs for controlling VR exposure duration

key_points.text: The duration of cyber sickness exposure depends on factors like virtual world size, travel speed, and interaction time.
Larger virtual environments naturally require a longer duration of VR exposure, while increasing travel speed reduces the time needed to explore.
Teleportation can reduce overall duration by allowing instantaneous movement, but it is not a natural movement.
Adjusting terrain distances can reduce travel time, but this approach prevents users from gaining a true sense of the real space and hampers mental map building.

key_terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition whose duration of exposure is determined by several factors, including the size of the virtual world, travelling speed, travelling time, and interaction time.
The duration of exposure is the time a user spends in the virtual environment, which can be reduced by controlling the speed of movement.
This movement involves instantaneous movement between two points, which reduces the overall duration of exposure.
A mental map is a construct whose difficulty in being built can hamper a user's ability to perform wayfinding activities in the virtual world.
A system-automated tool is one in which users do not interact.

segments.subgoal: Define the characteristics and scope of semi-interactive VR tours

key_points.text: The lecture focuses on semi-interactive tours, which do not totally disregard user interactions.
A semi-interactive tour is defined as interaction with Points of Interest (POIs) combined with navigation controlled by the system.
In this model, travel is automatic and system-controlled, but user interactions are limited only to designated POIs.
The objective of dealing with semi-interactive system control tools is to reduce the duration of exposure to the virtual world.

key_terms.definition: A tour characterized by interaction with Points of Interest (POIs) while navigation is controlled by the system.
Specific chosen points in the virtual environment where users are allowed to interact with objects.
Semi-interactive system control tools are the focus of our objective to reduce the duration of exposure to the virtual world.
A VR tool where the interaction time can be ignored because the system controls all aspects of the experience.

segments.subgoal: Compare two optimization approaches for designing efficient VR tours

key_points.text: Interaction time at points of interest can be limited by estimating the average time a user requires to interact with them.
One optimization approach seeks an optimum path that allows users to experience all points of interest in minimum total time.
The second optimization approach finds an optimum path to experience the maximum number of points of interest within a fixed time limit.
Both approaches address how to create an optimum VR tour where the duration of exposure is optimized.

key_terms.definition: A virtual tour where there is a limit placed on the time a user can spend interacting at a point of interest.
The total time a user spends in a virtual tour that needs to be optimized.

A path that allows users to interact with the maximum possible number of points of interest within a given fixed time.

segments.subgoal: Define the graph structure and objective for the optimal travel path problem

key_points.text: The virtual world is modeled as a weighted graph (G), where vertices (V) represent all Points of Interest (POIs) and edges (E) represent connections between them.
The weight of an edge is determined by the Euclidean distance between the two connected POIs.
The graph does not need to be complete because, in a realistic environment, a direct path between every pair of POIs may not exist.
The problem objective is to find a path that covers all vertices (POIs) while minimizing the time required and maintaining a realistic speed.

key_terms.definition: A single point of interest is a node or vertex in the graph representation of the virtual world.
The vertex set (V) represents all the points of interest within the virtual world.
The weighted edge set (E) consists of the weighted edges connecting all the points of interest.
The edge weight denotes the Euclidean distance between a pair of vertices, or a very large number if they are not directly connected.
Path P is the path within the graph that covers all vertices and minimizes the time required while maintaining a realistic speed.
